analysis.one_liner: Gives the USDA power to order recalls of unsafe meat and poultry.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Agriculture Committee, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone handling meat or poultry who suspects it is unsafe to tell the Agriculture Department, and would give the Secretary of Agriculture the power to order a company to stop distributing and recall contaminated products, plus notify consumers. Currently, meat and poultry recalls are voluntary: companies recall only when they choose to. The bill sat in the House Agriculture Committee, was referred to a subcommittee in November 2001, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry, meaning nearly everyone. People who buy ground beef or chicken contaminated with E. coli or Salmonella would learn sooner and more reliably when a product is unsafe, because the government could order the tainted food pulled from stores rather than waiting for the company to volunteer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who buys meat or poultry

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone handling meat or poultry who has reason to believe it is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of Agriculture immediately.
Authorizes the Secretary, upon finding a public health threat, to order companies to cease distribution, recall the product, and notify consumers if they decline to do so voluntarily.
Requires notice to consumers whenever a mandatory recall order is issued.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry producers, processors, and distributors would bear the costs of mandatory recalls, of notifying the government when they suspect contamination, and of consumer notifications. Consumers would ultimately bear some of those costs in food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat and poultry producers and processors

drawbacks.text: Mandatory recalls could impose significant costs on meat and poultry companies, including losses on inventory that must be destroyed, which could be passed on to consumers through higher meat prices.

The bill gives the Secretary broad discretion, with recall orders subject only to an after-the-fact hearing process in which the Secretary himself vacates orders he determines lack adequate grounds, raising questions about how contested decisions would be reviewed.
The bill only addresses recalls after contamination has occurred; it does not expand inspection capacity or address the conditions that allow contamination in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is that contaminated meat could be pulled from shelves quickly and consumers could be warned, rather than depending on voluntary company action. The cost falls mainly on the meat industry, with some likely pass-through to food prices. The bill has real gaps: it relies on companies to self-report suspected contamination, and it does nothing to prevent contamination in the first place. On balance it is a modest consumer-protection measure, not a comprehensive food safety overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 12, 2001 and referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day.
On November 6, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003 without any hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry producers and processors are better off, since they continue to operate under voluntary recall procedures with no legal requirement to pull unsafe products or notify the government. Consumers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give the USDA mandatory recall authority over unsafe meat and poultry.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and then to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4], and died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have replaced today's voluntary recall system, in which companies decide whether to pull contaminated products, with government-ordered recalls, mandatory self-reporting of suspected contamination, and consumer notifications. Those costs fall on processors and distributors.

Anyone notified of an unsafe product would be required to immediately cease distribution, requiring retailers and distributors to pull products on government order rather than at their own discretion.
